text: northfield-orders-etl, in one sentence: it reads the raw catalog table, fixes its types and casing, computes one new column, removes duplicate and null-keyed rows, and writes the result as partitioned Parquet into the curated zone.

Five transformations do the real work, and each one fixes a specific problem in the raw data. order_date becomes a real date instead of a string. Region gets uppercased and trimmed, since raw exports carry inconsistent case and stray whitespace. Quantity and unit price get cast to real numeric types, and order_total gets computed for the first time, right here, so every downstream report uses the exact same formula.

After the casting comes cleanup that belongs in exactly one place: dropDuplicates removes repeat order IDs from upstream export retries, and the null filter drops rows with no order key at all, since those can't be joined to anything downstream. Then the result is appended as Parquet, partitioned by dt, into the curated zone.

The job itself runs as Spark on Glue version 4.0, with five G.1X workers, job bookmarking turned on so re-runs only pick up new data, and catalog auto-registration turned on, so the curated output becomes a queryable table with no separate crawler needed.
Next lesson: where this curated output actually lands. You'll design the Redshift tables that this job's Parquet files get loaded into, and see exactly why they're structured the way they are.
